note: Causal-chain membership is based only on the supplied point-in-time evidence packet. Semantic equivalence does not require lexical similarity. PASS remains provisional until permutation consistency and evidence-ablation tests pass.

quarters.driver_name: Mobile/cloud data-consumption expansion
quarters.causal_chain: Growth in mobile Internet, connected applications and cloud usage -> more analytics/content traffic and cloud-compute demand -> higher demand for mobile analytics, digital content services and datacenter compute.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C16 is less explicit about the upstream mobile/cloud driver; edge is retained at lower confidence because its realized growth is in digital publishing/content-management services rather than merely generic company growth.

quarters.reason: Evidence contains isolated PC-form-factor, renewables/gas, broadband, e-commerce and customer-growth mechanisms, but no single upstream external driver is supported by >=4 companies across the required cluster structure.
Demand evidence is fragmented across construction products, bikes, hotels, medical devices and telecom; no common upstream external driver clears the breadth and cross-cluster rules.

Cloud infrastructure, biopharma, mortgage demand, semiconductors and consumer demand are present, but fewer than four companies support one evidence-grounded upstream chain without over-generalizing to 'economic growth'.
Optical networking, cloud infrastructure, automation, housing and energy-service demand are individually credible but do not form one sufficiently specific shared upstream causal chain.

quarters.driver_name: Online/cloud adoption expands bandwidth and digital-service deployment
quarters.causal_chain: More network-connected devices, cloud computing and online commerce -> higher bandwidth/network-upgrade demand and broader deployment of online/SaaS services -> higher e-commerce and subscription/service revenue.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: The downstream businesses differ, but all cited evidence points to realized expansion of online/cloud/network activity rather than generic internal growth.

quarters.reason: E-commerce/last-mile evidence appears in only a small subset; energy, tickets, coal, education and wireless evidence do not support one common driver with sufficient breadth.
Online commerce/payments, cloud capex, housing and hurricane-rebuild demand are heterogeneous; a shared 'digital growth' label would be too broad relative to the packet evidence.

quarters.driver_name: Cloud/data growth increases datacenter and semiconductor demand
quarters.causal_chain: Rapid growth of Internet/e-commerce/big data and cloud adoption -> greater datacenter power/compute and analytics requirements -> stronger semiconductor/wafer demand and data/analytics demand.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C20/C17 identify semiconductor/wafer demand but do not themselves state cloud as the sole cause; their edges are treated as downstream infrastructure exposure, not direct cloud-demand proof.

quarters.reason: One strong AI/datacenter demand edge exists, but the remaining evidence is spread across housing, energy, consulting, healthcare and regional sales; insufficient independent support for the same chain.
E-commerce distribution, graphite-electrode scarcity, pipelines and digital identity are separate mechanisms; no one upstream driver reaches four companies with cross-cluster support.
Graphite/steel, vehicle technology, pharmacy, weather and commercial real estate evidence are not one sufficiently specific common causal chain.

quarters.driver_name: Digitalization and e-commerce expand data, cloud and delivery infrastructure
quarters.causal_chain: More consumer and enterprise activity moves online -> data traffic, cloud usage, digital advertising and e-commerce GMV rise -> server capacity, parcel-delivery activity and digital monetization increase.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: Digital advertising and parcel logistics are different downstream nodes, but their cited business outcomes are explicitly tied to rising online activity rather than being grouped by vocabulary.

quarters.driver_name: Broadband/cloud and subscription-software adoption
quarters.causal_chain: Growing broadband/mobile-data use and enterprise migration to cloud/solution-based software -> greater network usage and hosted-service deployment -> higher data-service, subscription and cloud revenue.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: The evidence supports a shared adoption/migration mechanism; no edge relies on merely similar accounting or generic growth language.

quarters.driver_name: Migration of business and consumer activity to digital channels
quarters.causal_chain: Business processes, advertising and commerce increasingly move to digital/outsourced channels -> outsourced bank technology, digital advertising/display and e-commerce logistics demand increase.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C16 is forward-looking industrial commentary and therefore lower-directness; if its evidence is removed the driver may fail the minimum breadth test.

quarters.driver_name: Mainstream cloud/SaaS and app-platform adoption
quarters.causal_chain: Cloud-based always-on technology and digital application adoption become mainstream -> customers shift from on-premise software and offline services toward SaaS/cloud/app platforms -> recurring cloud/software/platform revenue scales.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C02 is digital-ad monetization rather than SaaS specifically, so it is a weaker downstream digital-platform edge.

quarters.driver_name: Early stay-at-home shock accelerates at-home/digital demand
quarters.causal_chain: COVID-related stay-at-home and off-premise behavior plus ongoing cloud adoption -> demand shifts toward at-home products, delivery and digital infrastructure -> higher digital/cloud capacity and selected at-home sales.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C13/C04 establish cloud/infrastructure expansion but do not independently attribute it to COVID; the common driver is therefore framed as the broader at-home/digital demand acceleration, not 'COVID caused AWS growth'.

quarters.driver_name: Remote-work and stay-at-home shift accelerates cloud and digital channels
quarters.causal_chain: Pandemic restrictions push work, consumption and sales online -> remote-work/cloud usage, digital fulfillment and delivery adoption rise -> higher cloud/platform/digital-channel demand.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: Some companies capture cost/fulfillment consequences rather than pure demand, but each cited edge reflects the same externally imposed shift toward remote/digital activity.

quarters.driver_name: Pandemic accelerates e-commerce and online-service adoption
quarters.causal_chain: Stay-at-home restrictions and property closures move shopping, entertainment and housing-search activity online -> e-commerce, digital betting, online retail and application adoption rise.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: The exact end markets differ, but the packet explicitly links each selected edge to pandemic-induced digital/at-home behavior.

quarters.driver_name: Persistent work-from-home and digital engagement
quarters.causal_chain: Work/learn/play-from-home behavior and digital-payment/app adoption remain elevated -> demand for mobile workstations, apps, digital payments and hosted software rises.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: Hosted-software and payments edges are broader digital-adoption exposures; the strongest direct evidence is the work-from-home computing/app behavior.

quarters.driver_name: Pandemic reallocates demand toward health, home and digital products
quarters.causal_chain: COVID changes health/sanitization needs, mobility and household behavior -> sanitizer/PPE/home-care demand rises, vehicle supply is disrupted and stay-at-home digital demand increases.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: This is one upstream pandemic shock with heterogeneous downstream transmissions; the graph does not claim the beneficiary products are substitutable or textually similar.

quarters.driver_name: Pandemic normalization and stimulus reshape mobility, consumer and system demand
quarters.causal_chain: Economic reopening/stimulus plus persistent at-home behavior -> vehicle scarcity/pricing, deferred medical-system purchases, pet-related spending, home-computing demand and freight congestion.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: The shared ancestor is pandemic/reopening behavior; downstream signs differ by industry, which is intentional in a causal-chain adjudication.

quarters.driver_name: Post-pandemic demand rebound meets semiconductor and supply constraints
quarters.causal_chain: Economic reopening and persistent digital/vehicle demand -> strong automotive/consumer demand while semiconductor/material capacity remains constrained -> higher prices/margins and supply shortages.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C09/C02 are broader reopening-demand edges; the semiconductor/material bottleneck is most direct in C16/C11 and automotive demand in C01/C08.

quarters.driver_name: Accelerated digitalization, 5G and HPC drive semiconductor/data-center demand
quarters.causal_chain: Digitalization, 5G and high-performance computing adoption accelerate -> demand for leading-edge semiconductors, networking, data-center equipment and related talent/capacity rises.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C11 is a broad data-center exposure and C22 is a labor-market transmission; both remain downstream nodes of the same semiconductor/digital-infrastructure expansion.

quarters.driver_name: Post-COVID energy-demand recovery collides with tight supply and geopolitical disruption
quarters.causal_chain: Economic reopening and recovering mobility/industrial activity lift oil, NGL and refined-product demand while supply remains tight and geopolitical disruption intensifies -> higher energy prices, margins, transport and service activity.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C23 is an oilfield-service/capex transmission rather than a commodity-price beneficiary and receives lower confidence.

quarters.driver_name: Pandemic-accelerated digitalization persists in semiconductors, e-commerce and cloud software
quarters.causal_chain: Work-from-home/stay-at-home behavior and broader digitalization -> higher device/semiconductor use, e-commerce/delivery penetration and cloud/software/payment adoption -> sustained digital-service and compute demand.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C07/C19 reflect general software/payment technology adoption and are weaker than the explicit pandemic/digitalization edges.

quarters.driver_name: Digitalization and cloud migration sustain semiconductor and SaaS demand
quarters.causal_chain: Persistent digitalization and cloud migration -> semiconductor/device demand and SMB SaaS adoption remain elevated -> component constraints, server/platform investment and cloud-software demand persist.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C05 is a cost/capacity consequence of marketplace growth rather than an explicit cloud-demand statement; it receives lower confidence.

quarters.reason: The packet contains isolated data-center/semiconductor, GLP-1, energy and specialty-product demand, but fewer than four independent companies support a single specific upstream driver.

quarters.driver_name: Digital transformation, 5G and HPC drive semiconductor capacity demand
quarters.causal_chain: 5G, AI/HPC and wider digital infrastructure adoption -> stronger demand across advanced/mature semiconductor nodes and automotive sensing -> manufacturers add wafer-fab capacity and production capability.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C26 is specifically ADAS adoption rather than all digital infrastructure and is therefore the weakest edge.

quarters.driver_name: Digital-first shift expands cybersecurity, semiconductor and automation infrastructure
quarters.causal_chain: Organizations move toward a digital-first operating model -> demand rises for security/network software, semiconductors/compute connectivity and industrial automation/robotics -> capital equipment and cloud-service demand expand.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C13 is cloud-services adoption in a financial platform rather than infrastructure demand and is retained only as a lower-directness downstream digitalization edge.

quarters.driver_name: Enterprise and consumer digital-platform adoption
quarters.causal_chain: Digital transformation, cloudification and AI adoption accelerate -> enterprises expand software/platform usage while consumers shift more activity to digital channels -> subscription and digital monetization demand rises.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: Only C03 explicitly names AI/cloudification; the broader accepted driver is digital-platform adoption, not an AI-specific theme.

quarters.reason: Generative-AI/GPU demand is explicit in one company, but the rest of the packet does not provide >=3 additional independent companies with evidence-grounded exposure to the same upstream driver.
Cloud-platform, server, utility-infrastructure and GLP-1 demand appear, but no specific upstream driver is evidenced by four companies across the required B2 communities.

quarters.driver_name: Enterprise cloud/data-platform adoption with emerging AI infrastructure spend
quarters.causal_chain: Organizations increase use of cloud, SaaS, data-driven services and AI-optimized infrastructure -> more installed-base service revenue, hosting usage and cloud transaction volume, with AI beginning to redirect infrastructure spending.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: Only C09 directly attributes spending to AI; the official driver remains broader cloud/data-platform adoption rather than retroactively labeling all members as AI beneficiaries.

quarters.reason: Evidence is fragmented across mortgages, chicken demand, cyber security, building products, gaming and digital assets; no common external driver meets the breadth rule.
AI/data-center demand is direct for only a small subset; oilfield, healthcare, agriculture, media and banking evidence cannot be joined without narrative overreach.

quarters.driver_name: AI/cloud data-center buildout increases compute and power-infrastructure demand
quarters.causal_chain: AI and mainstream cloud adoption -> more data-processing loads and data-center construction -> higher demand for AI platforms, cloud services and electrical/power infrastructure.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C18 is cloud-adoption exposure without explicit data-center power linkage; it is retained as an upstream digital-demand node at lower confidence.

quarters.driver_name: AI data-center buildout propagates into networking, electrical infrastructure and grid/storage demand
quarters.causal_chain: Accelerated AI compute adoption -> rapid data-center/network buildout -> demand expands for high-speed networking, datacenter enclosures/electrical projects and grid/storage infrastructure.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C10/C01 are grid-storage demand nodes and do not explicitly name AI; they are accepted only as downstream infrastructure exposure, with lower confidence than the networking/datacenter edges.

quarters.driver_name: AI compute expansion raises memory, storage, electricity and technology-material demand
quarters.causal_chain: Large-language-model and generative-AI adoption -> greater memory/storage and hyperscale infrastructure needs -> higher information-sector electricity use and technology-material demand.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C12's masked 'information' sector does not explicitly say AI/data centers; it is the weakest infrastructure edge and should be highly sensitive to evidence ablation.

quarters.reason: One company has strong next-generation AI/datacom demand, but the remaining evidence is mostly defense, healthcare, energy, e-commerce logistics and finance; insufficient four-company AI causal chain.

quarters.driver_name: AI/cloud data-center expansion creates a time-to-power and digital-infrastructure buildout
quarters.causal_chain: Adoption of AI tools, cloud computing and digital technologies -> more hyperscale/data-center capacity -> higher server, power, edge/digital-platform and supporting material demand.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C20 is anticipated demand and C11/C07 are broad digital/edge adoption; the causal core is C13/C26. Permutation and ablation tests are expected to challenge the weaker outer edges.

quarters.driver_name: AI-driven HPC buildout propagates through servers, semiconductors and fab/packaging equipment
quarters.causal_chain: AI/ML application demand -> rapid HPC/GPU-server and networking buildout -> higher semiconductor-chip demand -> higher advanced-packaging and semiconductor environmental/equipment demand.
quarters.counterevidence_and_caveats: C07 names semiconductor demand rather than AI directly, but its position as a downstream fab-support exposure is supported by the same-quarter AI-driven semiconductor evidence from other independent companies.
